name: Amira Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter for Calder Construction, one of the big commercial contractors, and right now we're building a new wing on the hospital out by the ring road. I do a bit of everything timber: temporary works, door sets, the boxing-in around pipes, and lately a lot of checking positions on the tablet. The whole building is in a 3D model, which is basically a computer version of the building you can spin around, so I'll stand in a bare concrete room and see on the screen exactly where the wall should go. I like that bit, it feels like a game. What wears me out is the walk from the canteen to level five, twice a day, because the lift is always full of plasterers.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Josh, he's a line chef, so his hours are as weird as mine. We're renting a small place and I took a loan for a used car last year, so savings are basically nothing, less than a month. Calder is a big name but I came in through an agency, so my rate's lower than the people on staff, and there aren't many big sites near us between jobs. I use AI every day, honestly, for everything from reading specifications to planning my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Kind of a letdown, but fine for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a useful tool, just not the revolution people promised. I'd tell people on site it saved me loads of time reading specs, and the older lads would roll their eyes. Online I'd post a few honest reviews of the tools that were actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and my path is the same as now. I want to move into setting-out, that's the person who marks out where everything goes on site using a laser instrument called a total station. That was my plan with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Calder and push to get off the agency and onto staff, because that's real money. I'd ask the setting-out engineer, Femi, if I could shadow him for a few weeks. I'd keep using AI for the boring bits, specs and emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older lads would roll their eyes. Do you get that a lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. Young, a woman, always on a tablet, I tick every box for them. But when they need to find a pipe position on the model, they come and ask me. I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does getting onto staff mean for you and Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holiday pay, sick pay, a pension, and maybe twenty percent more. It'd mean we could pay the car loan off early and actually save. That's the big thing for me in the next year, whatever happens with AI.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a useful tool, just not the revolution people promised. I'd tell people on site it saved me time reading specifications and post honest reviews online of the tools that worked.
S0.think: Privately it means my job's safe and my path stays the same. I want to move into setting-out, marking where everything goes on site with a laser instrument, with or without AI.
S0.do: Keeps working at Calder and pushes to move from agency to staff. Asks the setting-out engineer if she can shadow him and keeps using AI for specifications and emails.
S0.quote: Young, a woman, always on a tablet, I tick every box for them.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is already the person on site who reads the 3D model for others. Her goals, getting off agency pay and into setting-out, don't depend on AI at all. Her thin savings come from a car loan and agency rates rather than poor habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like where I already think it's going. I'm kind of ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to learn, and that firms should train people instead of just hiring in. I wouldn't get political about it. I'd tell the younger ones on site to get comfortable with the tablets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this would be good for me. Setting-out is already half technology, and site robots that print layout lines on the floor would need someone to set them up and check them. That's exactly the job I'm aiming at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a setting-out course at the college in the first few months, it's evenings, and pay for it out of the car money if I had to. I'd learn the layout robots the first time Calder got one on site. I'd keep a bit of money back, but I'd rather spend on skills than sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, with a small voice in my head saying don't get cocky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't get cocky. What's that voice warning you about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm on agency pay and they can drop me with a day's notice. Being good with tech doesn't help if you're the first one they cut when a contract ends. I've seen it happen to people better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tony, the carpenter who does the temporary works. He's brilliant with his hands, can't use a phone. If his work moves to a factory, he'd be lost, and he's too proud to ask for help.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to learn, and that firms should train people instead of hiring in. I wouldn't get political, and I'd tell younger workers to get comfortable with tablets now.
S1.think: Privately I think this would be good for me, because setting-out is already half technology. Site robots that print layout lines would need someone to set them up and check them, which is exactly my goal.
S1.do: Signs up for an evening setting-out course within months, paying from car money if needed. Learns layout robots as soon as Calder brings one on site and spends on skills before savings.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with a small warning voice not to get cocky.
S1.quote: Being good with tech doesn't help if you're the first one they cut when a contract ends.
S1.fieldNote: Amira sees this picture as matching her plans almost exactly. Her one real worry is her agency status, not the technology. She thinks of a skilled older colleague, Big Tony, who would struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's my plan getting run over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, fast, about how robots come onto sites, safety rules and something to help people who lose work. I'd say both the government and the companies need to sort it out together. I'd post about it, but I'd try not to sound like I was panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd have a year, maybe eighteen months, as one of the people who sets up and checks the robots. After that, the robots set each other up. And I'm on agency pay with a car loan, so when that work goes, it goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every system that came on site, the first week, so I was the obvious person to keep. I'd sell the car and pay off the loan before things got bad. I'd try to pick up side work too, helping smaller firms get their robots and software running, because they'd be lost and they'd pay someone to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I'm running for a train that's already moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would smaller firms really pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. A five-man firm buys a layout robot and nobody knows how to calibrate it. I'd charge by the day. It wouldn't last past the time the robots set themselves up, but it'd keep me going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Josh say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh would say kitchens are safe, people want a person cooking. I'd say I'm not sure about that either. We'd probably decide to keep renting and not do anything big, no moves, no wedding talk, until we knew.

S2.say: I'd say we need fast rules for robots on sites, covering safety and help for people who lose work, with government and companies sorting it out together. I'd post about it without sounding panicked.
S2.think: Privately I'd have a year or eighteen months as someone who sets up and checks the robots, and then they'd set each other up. On agency pay with a car loan, that work would go fast.
S2.do: Learns every new site system in its first week so she's the obvious one to keep. Sells the car to clear the loan and picks up paid side work helping small firms set up robots and software.
S2.feel: Anxious, like running for a train that's already moving.
S2.quote: Like I'm running for a train that's already moving.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Amira under real pressure but still acting, not frozen. She sees a short window of work setting up robots for small firms and is realistic that it closes. She and Josh would put big life steps on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually finish things. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so firms should be training people now, not in year four. I'd say the colleges should be teaching robot setup and site technology to anyone who wants it. I'd be pretty positive about it, publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is probably enough to get into setting-out properly and then move up to managing the robot side on a big site. That might last a few years past 2031. I'd be honest though, I don't really know what happens after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setting-out course in the first year and then a second course in site technology or surveying. I'd get off agency onto staff, pay off the car, and try to have two or three months saved by year three. I'd buy a second-hand survey drone and learn it at weekends, because measuring sites from the air is going to be big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel busy. Busy's good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A drone isn't cheap. Is that wise on less than a month of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not in year one. Maybe year two, once the car's paid off. I'd find a used one, a few hundred. It's a bet, but it's a small one, and I'm okay with small bets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to switch from being a carpenter who's good with tablets to being a technology person who used to be a carpenter. That's a real change, and you can't do it in two years.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so firms should train people now, not in year four, and colleges should teach robot setup and site technology to anyone who wants it. I'd be positive about it publicly.
S3.think: Privately five years is probably enough to get into setting-out and then manage the robot side on a big site, which might last a few years past 2031. I don't really know what happens after that.
S3.do: Takes a setting-out course in the first year and then a site technology or surveying course. Moves from agency to staff, clears the car loan, and later buys a used survey drone to learn at weekends.
S3.feel: Slightly uneasy but mostly busy, which suits her.
S3.quote: Time to switch from being a carpenter who's good with tablets to being a technology person who used to be a carpenter.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Amira plan a full shift in identity, from carpenter to site technology worker. She accepts small, measured risks like a used drone once her loan is paid. She is honest that she can't see past the early 2030s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole second career, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be silly to waste it. Train people, help the ones who can't switch, make sure small firms aren't wiped out. I'd say it at work and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels good for me. I'd have time to become a setting-out engineer, then a site technology lead, then maybe run my own small survey business. The end point is still a question mark, but I'd have a decade of better pay first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the courses one at a time over three or four years, no rush. I'd get onto staff at Calder and save properly. Around year three I'd start a weekend survey business with a drone, small jobs, house extensions, and see if it grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a question mark at the end, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start a business. Is that something you've thought about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Since I was twenty, honestly. My mum ran a little alterations shop, sewing, and I grew up doing her invoices. I like the idea of being my own boss. Ten years is enough to try it and fail once and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end point is a question mark. Does that stop you sleeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's ten years away, and by then I'd hope there's some kind of plan for everyone. If there isn't, I'd be in the same boat as everybody else, at least with some savings.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be silly to waste it: train people, help those who can't switch, and make sure small firms aren't wiped out. I'd say it at work and mean it.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels good for me, with time to become a setting-out engineer, a site technology lead and maybe run my own survey business. The end point is a question mark, but I'd get a decade of better pay first.
S4.do: Takes courses one at a time over three or four years, moves onto staff at Calder and saves properly. Around year three starts a weekend drone survey business for small jobs like house extensions.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a question mark at the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to try it and fail once and try again.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Amira lets herself think about a long-held wish to run her own business, rooted in her mother's alterations shop. She is comfortable with the uncertainty at the end because she expects a shared problem by then. Her calm comes from time and adaptability, despite her thin savings today.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be on agency pay with a car loan and the window to switch would close before I got through it. What would help is free, fast courses in the new site technology, and firms having to keep agency people on long enough to retrain. Some help with the bills while you train would make a big difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about agency workers. Half the people on a big site are agency, like me. We're the easiest to drop, and nobody counts us when they talk about job losses. I'd want someone to count us.

headlineQuote: We're the easiest to drop, and nobody counts us when they talk about job losses.
portrait: Amira Chen is a 27-year-old agency site carpenter on a hospital build for a big contractor, living with her chef boyfriend Josh, paying off a used-car loan and holding less than a month of savings. She uses AI every day and is the person on site who reads the 3D building model for others. She is calm about the plateau and steady disruption, which fit her plan to move into setting-out, and anxious at AGI in two years because her agency status and loan would leave her little time. With five or ten years she plans a shift into site technology and even a small drone survey business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because on agency pay with a car loan the window to switch careers would close before she got through it.
whatWouldHelp: Free, fast courses in new site technology, rules making firms keep agency workers long enough to retrain, and help with bills during training.
